scope.flow: Covenant.multicall nested invocation desynchronizes the contract-wide _isMulticall guard, causing subsequent outer batch items to enforce payment equality and revert
scope.environment: Solidity smart contract (Covenant) using MulticallLib delegatecall batching

statements.text: An outer Covenant.multicall batch is being executed, with _isMulticall set to true before delegating into MulticallLib.multicall.
A payload item in the outer batch invokes Covenant.multicall again (nested invocation), directly or indirectly through helper calls.
The outer batch contains subsequent items that follow the nested invocation and are still part of the original multicall.
Payment-sensitive entrypoints updateState, mint, redeem, and swap rely on _checkPayment(msgValue) to skip msg.value == msgValue enforcement during batched execution.
The nested multicall invocation flips _isMulticall back to true and, when the nested batch unwinds, resets the flag to false while the outer batch is still iterating.
Subsequent outer batch items execute with _isMulticall == false even though they are still part of the original multicall.

Covenant.multicall unconditionally clears the contract-wide _isMulticall flag to false once the delegatecall returns, so a nested invocation's unwind resets the flag while the outer batch is still iterating.

While an outer multicall batch is executing, _isMulticall must remain true for the entire batch so that payment-sensitive entrypoints consistently skip msg.value == msgValue enforcement for all items in the batch.
A nested multicall invocation must not alter the guard state observed by the remaining items of the enclosing outer batch.
Otherwise valid delegated batch sequences that include a nested multicall must not be turned into guaranteed reverts for the remainder of the outer sequence.
Nested multicalls cause outer batch items that follow the nested invocation to revert with `Errors.E_IncorrectPayment`, halting execution and wasting gas.
Integrations that rely on delegated batching (e.g., routers that compose protocol actions) can be griefed by inserting a nested `multicall`, turning otherwise valid sequences into guaranteed reverts.
Because the final balance check only triggers after the outer batch finishes, the DoS effect persists for the remainder of the transaction without any post-hoc recovery.

ambiguities: Report does not specify a concrete attacker actor or permission; griefing is described as inserting a nested multicall but no explicit unauthorized-caller statement is given.
Report does not state whether the nested invocation is intentional or accidental in the triggering scenario.
Exact number or identity of remaining outer batch items is not specified.
